Capsule & trabeculae.description: The spleen is wrapped in a thin outer capsule of dense connective tissue, covered over most of its surface by mesothelium (the visceral layer of the peritoneum). Trabeculae are connective-tissue partitions that branch inward from the capsule and carry blood vessels into the organ, forming the spleen's supporting framework.
clinical: The capsule is thin and encloses a soft, blood-rich organ, so a blow to the left upper abdomen can tear it and cause serious internal bleeding.

White pulp.description: White pulp is the lymphoid tissue of the spleen. It holds T-cell zones around the central arterioles (the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath) and B-cell follicles, where immune cells screen blood-borne antigens and make antibodies. Germinal centres inside follicles are where B cells multiply and refine their antibodies during an immune response.
clinical: White pulp helps clear encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococci. After the spleen is removed, people remain at risk of severe infection by these bacteria, so vaccines are usually given beforehand.

Follicular surface.description: The marginal zone is the outer border of each white pulp follicle, where white pulp meets red pulp. It contains marginal-zone B cells and blood-filled spaces that catch blood-borne antigens. In humans this border is open rather than the neat ring of lined vessels seen in rodents.

Red pulp.description: Red pulp is the filtering part of the spleen. Blood flows from small arteries into open splenic cords, where macrophages remove old or damaged red cells, and then drains into venous sinuses; it is named for the many red cells it holds.

Vessels.description: Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery, which branches into trabecular arteries. Central arterioles run through the white pulp and continue as penicillar arterioles that open into the red pulp. Blood leaves through pulp veins and trabecular veins, which join the splenic vein and carry it to the portal vein.
clinical: In cirrhosis and other causes of high portal pressure, blood backs up in the splenic vein, so the spleen becomes congested and enlarged (splenomegaly) and can trap blood cells, causing hypersplenism.

Filtering detail - enlarged schematic.description: Splenic venous sinuses are lined by long, rod-like endothelial cells (stave cells), with narrow slits between them. Flexible, healthy red cells can squeeze through these slits into the sinus, while stiff or aged red cells are held back in the cords, where macrophages remove them.
clinical: Stiff or misshapen red cells, such as spherocytes in hereditary spherocytosis, are trapped in the red pulp and destroyed there. Removing the spleen often helps these patients.
Sickled red cells can clog the slits and cords of the red pulp, causing repeated small infarcts that can shrink the spleen and leave the patient functionally asplenic.

parts.description: Mesothelium is the single layer of flat, thin cells on the spleen's outer surface, continuous with the visceral peritoneum that wraps the abdominal organs. It makes the surface smooth and glistening, so the organ can slide easily against neighbouring structures during breathing. It is absent at the hilum, where the splenic vessels enter and leave, and in a section it shows as a thin line of flat nuclei at the outer edge.

The capsule is the tough outer wall of the spleen, made of dense connective tissue rich in collagen, with elastic fibres and some smooth muscle. Its outer surface is wrapped in mesothelium, except at the hilum where the vessels enter. In a section it appears as a dense, pink-staining band at the margin of the organ, from which the trabeculae extend inward. A blow to the left upper abdomen can tear it, causing internal bleeding.

The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) is a cuff of T lymphocytes that surrounds the central arteriole in the white pulp, next to the B-cell follicles. It is the T-cell zone of the spleen, where T cells respond to blood-borne antigens presented by dendritic cells. In a section it is recognised as a dense, darkly stained ring of small lymphocytes wrapped around a small artery.

Splenic follicles are rounded nodules of B lymphocytes in the white pulp, and they appear as dark, round masses in a section. The mantle zone is the dense ring of small, resting B cells that surrounds the germinal centre, so it forms a dark crown around the paler centre of the follicle. Follicles are the spleen's B-cell zones, where antibody-producing immune responses are organised.

A germinal centre is the pale, round area inside an activated splenic follicle where B lymphocytes multiply rapidly after meeting an antigen. The dividing B cells refine their antibodies to fit the antigen more tightly, helped by follicular dendritic cells that hold antigen on their surface. In a section it is a light-staining centre encircled by the darker mantle zone, and it is prominent when the spleen is responding to infection.

Perifollicular open spaces are the blood-filled gaps in the marginal zone that surround the outer edge of each white pulp follicle. In humans these spaces are not lined by the continuous vessel wall seen in rodents, so blood moves through them slowly and blood-borne antigens are trapped by marginal-zone macrophages and B cells. In a section they look like pale, open spaces between the follicle and the red pulp.

The superficial follicular zone is the outer part of a white pulp follicle, the band of B lymphocytes that faces the marginal zone and red pulp rather than the central arteriole. It is made mainly of small lymphocytes and forms the transition from the dense follicle into the more open marginal zone. In a section it is recognised at the edge of the follicle, just before the paler marginal zone.

Venous sinusoids, also called venous sinuses, are the wide, thin-walled channels of the red pulp that receive blood from the splenic cords and drain it into pulp veins. Their wall is formed by rod-shaped stave cells lying side by side. In a section they appear as irregular, blood-filled channels, with the elongated nuclei of the stave cells visible along the wall.

Ring fibres are circular bundles of fine reticular fibres that encircle each venous sinus in the red pulp, lying outside the stave cells and their basement membrane. They give the thin sinus wall mechanical support, so the sinus does not collapse or over-stretch as blood passes through. In a silver-stained section they appear as fine, ring-shaped fibres around the sinuses.

Trabeculae are fibrous partitions that extend inward from the capsule, made of dense connective tissue with elastic fibres and smooth muscle cells. They divide the spleen's interior into incomplete compartments and carry the trabecular arteries and veins, which enter at the hilum and branch into the pulp. In a section they show as fibrous strands with thick-walled vessels lying between areas of pulp.

Trabecular arteries are the larger branches of the splenic artery that run inside the trabeculae from the hilum into the organ. They have a thick smooth-muscle wall and give off the central arterioles that enter the white pulp. In a section they appear as round, thick-walled muscular arteries lying in the trabeculae beside the thinner-walled trabecular vein.

Trabecular veins run within the trabeculae alongside the trabecular arteries, collecting blood from the pulp veins and carrying it out of the spleen. They drain into the splenic vein at the hilum, which carries blood on to the portal vein. In a section they are thin-walled vessels beside a trabecular artery, with a much less muscular wall than the artery.

The central arteriole, also called the central artery, is the small artery that runs through each white pulp nodule, usually sheathed by T cells (PALS) and set off-centre within it. Follicular branches arise from it to supply the surrounding B-cell follicle. In a section it appears as a small, round, thick-walled artery sitting off-centre in a lymphoid nodule.

Penicillar arterioles are the small, brush-like branches of the central arteriole that carry blood into the red pulp; the name comes from the Latin penicillus, a painter's brush. Their wall is still muscular, and they divide into fine branches before ending as sheathed capillaries. In a section they appear as small, thick-walled arterioles lying in the red pulp, away from the white pulp.

Sheathed capillaries are the thin, end-stage arterial vessels of the red pulp, continuous with the penicillar arterioles. Each is wrapped in a dense cuff of macrophages and reticular fibres, the Schweigger-Seidel sheath, which traps antigens and particles from the blood. Blood leaving them passes into the open splenic cords. In a section they look like small capillary-sized vessels with a thick, dense sheath around them.

Pulp veins are the small veins of the red pulp that collect blood from the venous sinuses and drain it into the larger trabecular veins. They lie within the red pulp rather than in the trabeculae, and they carry blood onward towards the splenic vein and the portal vein. In a section they appear as small, thin-walled vessels in the red pulp, frequently holding red cells.

The splenic cords, also called the cords of Billroth, are the cell-filled strands of red pulp that lie between the venous sinuses. They form a meshwork of reticular fibres and reticular cells that holds red cells, macrophages, plasma cells, lymphocytes and granulocytes. Blood percolates slowly through the cords before entering the sinuses, and macrophages in the cords remove old or damaged red cells.

Sinus endothelial staves, or stave cells, are the long, rod-shaped endothelial cells that form the wall of the splenic venous sinus. They lie side by side, parallel to the length of the sinus, and narrow slits separate neighbouring cells. Their elongated nuclei show as a row of dark ovals along the sinus wall in a section.

The discontinuous basement membrane is the incomplete layer that forms hoop-like rings around the stave cells of the sinus wall, rather than a continuous sheet. It is made of the usual basement membrane proteins, type IV collagen and laminin, and it stains with PAS in a section. Together with the slits between staves, its gaps let blood cells pass from the cords into the sinus.

The cord reticular scaffold is the meshwork of reticular fibres and reticular cells that fills the splenic cords outside the venous sinuses. Its fibres are made of type III collagen, and they support the mixed population of blood cells and macrophages in the cords. In a silver-stained section it appears as a fine, lacy network threading through the cord tissue.

keys: Inset: red cells in cord space
parts.description: Red blood cells in the cord space are cells that have left the terminal arterioles and are slowly squeezing through the cord tissue before reaching the sinuses. They sit among macrophages, plasma cells and lymphocytes, making the cords a dense cellular region. Their slow passage is what allows macrophages to detect and remove damaged cells.

keys: Inset: flexible red cell at true stave gap
parts.description: A flexible red cell passing a stave gap is a healthy erythrocyte (red blood cell) that folds its disc shape to squeeze through the narrow slit between two stave cells into the sinus. Healthy red cells are highly deformable because of their membrane and internal cytoskeleton. The slit is narrower than the resting cell, so the cell must bend to pass through it.

keys: Inset: red cells in sinus lumen
parts.description: Red blood cells in the sinus lumen are cells that have passed the stave slits and are now carried in the venous sinus towards the pulp veins. The sinus is a wide, low-pressure channel, so the cells flow more freely here than in the crowded cords. In a section the lumen appears as an open space filled with red cells, bounded by the thin sinus wall.

A cord macrophage is a large phagocytic cell (one that engulfs debris) of the red pulp, lying among the splenic cords, that removes old, damaged or antibody-coated red cells. It is a key cell in recycling haemoglobin iron from broken-down red cells. Its cytoplasm often contains red cell debris, and in a section it appears as a large cell with an irregular outline among the red cells.

The nucleus of a cord macrophage holds the cell's genetic material and is usually oval or kidney-shaped, with finely dispersed chromatin. This shape and pale staining help separate it from the small, round, dark nucleus of a lymphocyte. In a section, the macrophage nucleus is a clue to recognising the cell among the red cells.

keys: Inset: rigid red cell retained for clearance
parts.description: A rigid red cell retained for clearance is an old, stiff or damaged erythrocyte that cannot deform enough to pass the narrow stave slits into the sinus. Its membrane has lost flexibility, so it stays in the cord, where macrophages recognise and remove it. This is one of the spleen's most important roles in clearing aged red cells from the blood.

The open terminal arterial capillary is the final arterial segment of the red pulp, where arterial branches open directly into the cords rather than into a closed capillary bed. This open type of circulation means blood passes through the cord tissue before entering the sinuses. In a section it appears as a thin-walled vessel that ends abruptly in cord tissue, rather than joining a sinus.

The venous outflow sleeve is the outflow end of a splenic venous sinus, where the sinus empties into a pulp vein that carries blood out of the red pulp. Its lumen is patent, meaning it stays open, so blood can leave the red pulp freely. In a section it appears as a segment of sinus wall with a clear lumen, continuous with a pulp vein.
